I would like to thank Robert Hoca for being attentive to our questions and problems, he was very quick to answer our emails whenever we had to solve a problem. He was also ready to create time for us.  If I may, there are a couple of suggestions that I would like to make.
I  think that my biggest criticism for this course would be time. I don't know if this is a general issue for this course or it is just a planning problem, but we had very little time to both conduct and analyze our study, and to write our final report.  We've had other lessons that revolved around a group project, and it followed a route in which all of the students and the instructor met for the first couple of weeks to talk about what they were expected to do. Thereafter, those collective meetings turned into 15-20 minute "group" meetings. So there would only be the instructor and the group itself -not the entire class- and the instructor and the group would discuss their shortcomings, what they have done, etc. for the study. We were much more comfortable and we were able to use time much more efficiently. I don't know if this format is suitable for this course, but I would've appreciated it so much if we only had meetings when it was necessary and when it was kept short.
I also think that we spent too much time analyzing other datasets, and their feedbacks took a long time as well. I think that unless a student asks for a one-on-one meeting, sending the feedback via email is the best option, instead of doing it with the entire class.
Also, I believe that Robert Hoca did not have enough information about the processes as well. A lot of times it felt like the students learned what they were supposed to do at the same time as Robert Hoca. I do not mean any insolence with this statement, please don't get me wrong. However, this, unfortunately, became an issue especially when we ran into a problem.
That is all I wanted to say. I would like to once again thank Robert Hoca for his efforts and time.

First and foremost, the instructor's insistence on group work and the fact that nearly the entire course grade is based on group projects is a major issue. The excuse that "the professional or academic world requires group work, so we are teaching that" is not valid because in the real world, people who rely on the work of others without contributing face consequences. Here, there is no peer evaluation, not even a symbolic one. As is well-known, if individual effort within a group is not assessed, people tend to freeload.

Looking at the syllabus, the grading breakdown shows that theoretically only 30% of the grade is group work. The instructor claims that "only 30% of the grade is group work, and no one can survive with just 30%, so freeloading is not an issue." However, in practice, individual components such as the introduction can be written based on the group project's introduction with minor modifications. The methods section in the individual final report can be copied directly from the group project's methods. Presentations, which are group work, include the results section, allowing students to write their individual results based on the group presentation. Even participation activities, which are supposed to be individual, often involve group work.

Contrary to what the instructor says, a significant portion of this course involves group work, and without any monitoring or meaningful peer evaluation, the workload falls disproportionately on one person, making it a torturous experience.

I feel like a lot of the aspects of the course are unfair with the group work taken into account, especially if you are taking on the brunt of the work in your group. This increases the workload significantly, so much so that I ended up dreading deadlines because I knew I’d be doing the work of 3-4 people all by myself, which ended up worsening my performance on all other courses. In addition, the high amount of statistics knowledge we’re required to possess before learning the topics in the statistics course feels weird to me.
